translations.text: A letter of [?] in the Spirit—that is, the subject of this letter above. To the true believer and lover of God:
Our spiritual father, the priest Mar Barlahe, who lives enclosed in hope in the Lord, in the enclosure of Mar Elisha of Markabta; from the sinful and lowly man who needs God's mercy and the help

of your prayers, Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Our Lady Mary, the Mother of God, in Beth Liqnis: abundant and most excellent greetings in our Lord Jesus Christ, the true and eternally existing God.

After this greeting, my lord, I appeal to your godly love to remember us continually in your prayers that are accepted before God. For I have truly experienced in my own person the effective help of your prayers, and for this reason
I continually ask in faith for the prayers of your fatherhood. For when I previously received the letter of your kindness, which urged me to translate this book from Greek into Syriac,

I could not find within myself even a single sound and vigorous thought ready for this excellent work. I did not think at all that I was capable of this task, and for this reason I had never even considered undertaking it. But when the letter of your holiness, together with your prayer, visited me
through our chaste brother, the deacon Mar Damian, what once happened to the paralyzed man, when they lowered him on a bed from the roof before our Lord Jesus, happened to me as well.
For just as, in that case, because of the faith of those who brought that paralyzed man to our Lord,
he was granted forgiveness of his sins and healing of his body, so I believe that because of your faith and your diligence,

our Lord has now also visited my soul and my thoughts, so that they may gain strength against the sickness of lethargy, be invigorated out of their paralysis, and be enlightened for this excellent work. This is not because I was capable or worthy of it, but for the benefit of the many who love learning
and for the praise of his divinity. Now, therefore, my lord, with his help and in hope in the good physician of our souls, our souls and our bodies, our Lord Jesus Christ,

who is the cause, beginning, and perfecter of all good things, I have devoted myself, in accordance with your fatherhood's encouragement, to translating this book from Greek into Syriac. I ask your fatherhood and everyone who encounters it not to let your mind become troubled

or disturbed when you find in it expressions or names that differ from the Syriac tradition and are also foreign to the arrangement of speech to which we Syrians are accustomed. For I took great care, as far as I could,
to translate them into Syriac as precisely as possible and just as the expressions are stated in the Greek language, even if the language does not flow and is not arranged
as Syrians are accustomed to it. This was so that the meaning of the expressions might be understood in agreement and harmony with the explanation that the teacher gave of them.
Furthermore, I inform your love that in one of the copies of this book I found written above it: “A scholion of the blessed Athanasius.”

It has kinship and fellowship with the other books. Furthermore, it has this particular [?] marvel: it contains, written down, the movements of every soul, these changes, and the ways of setting them right,
and they are depicted in it so that anyone who wishes may take a model from it and reflect, being himself formed in the way described there. In the other books, a person hears the law,

which commands only what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. He hears the prophecies only so that he may recognize the Christ who is coming, and he looks into the histories so that from them he can learn the deeds of kings

and holy people. But in the Book of Psalms, besides learning these things, the hearer also finds in it the movements of his own soul. He thus learns both what he feels and what holds him in its grip, and he can also receive from it a model

of words, and learn how he ought to speak and act to heal his suffering. For in those other books there are words that prohibit and cut off wrongdoing, but in this book the way one ought to turn away from it is also depicted. For example, [?]
there is a command to repent. Repenting itself means ceasing from sin. But here, how one ought to repent and what one ought to say in repentance are also depicted. Again, Paul says that affliction

produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame. But in the Psalms there is also how we ought to endure afflictions and what we ought to say when we are afflicted.

And what comes after affliction, and how everyone is tested, and what words belong to those who hope in the Lord. It is also written and laid down as a command that we should give thanks in everything. But the Psalms teach us what we ought to say when giving thanks, just as we also learn by hearing others.
We learn from the Psalms that all who wish to live in the fear of God are persecuted, and how we ought to think when we flee, and what words those who are persecuted ought to offer to God.

After persecution, when they have been delivered, we are commanded to bless God and give him thanks. But in the Psalms we are also given a pattern for how we ought to praise God, and what words we should say to give thanks fittingly.
For every circumstance a person can find divine songs of praise suited to us, to our feelings, and to our condition. For this too is remarkable about the Psalms: in the other books, those things

that the saints say, and the people about whom they say these things—those who read make known whom these things concern. Those who hear consider the people being spoken about to be different from themselves,
and these deeds that are made known serve to make them marvel at them and [?] toward imitating them. But someone who takes up this book receives the prophecies about the Savior in the same way

as in the other books, and goes away marveling and worshiping. But he reads the other words as though they were his own. The listener, as though he himself were speaking, [?], and at the same time takes his place among the words of praise

as though they were his own. For the sake of clarity, I ought not to hesitate, like the blessed apostle, to repeat the same thing. Beginning again, I say: there are many words of the patriarchs, words spoken by them that belong particularly to them.
Moses would speak, and God would answer him. Elijah and Elisha, while staying on Mount Carmel, would call upon the Lord and would always say,
“As the Lord lives, before whom I have stood today.” The words of the other holy prophets are primarily about Christ, but after that many concern
the nations and Israel as well. Yet no one has ever spoken even the words of the patriarchs as his own, nor does anyone dare to imitate Moses and speak his words
as his own words, or those of Abraham concerning the man born in his household and Ishmael,

or those concerning the great Isaac. Even if the very same need should overtake someone, [?] he dares to speak them as his own. But even if someone shares the suffering of those who suffer, and at times feels a longing

for that virtuous man, he never says, like Moses, “Reveal yourself to me,” or again, “If you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if you do not forgive them, blot me out of your book that you have written.”
Nor does someone take up the words of the prophets as his own words and use them to rebuke people or praise those who have done things resembling those for which the prophets rebuked or praised them.

Nor does anyone imitate the saying, “As the Lord lives, before whom I have stood today,” and speak it as his own statement. For it is clear that someone reading the books speaks these words not as his own,
but as belonging to the saints and to those made known through him. But the remarkable thing about the words of the Psalms is this: after the prophecies about the Savior and the nations,
the person who says the other words speaks them as his own.

Everyone sings as though these things had been written about him. He does not receive them and go away as though they were said to make something known about someone else. Rather, he takes his place as though speaking about himself, and according

to the nature of what is said, he offers these things to God as though he himself had done them and were speaking from his own heart. For these words are not taken in the same way as the words of the patriarchs, Moses,
and the other prophets. Instead, he confidently speaks and sings these words as his own and as written about him. For the Psalms embrace both the person who keeps the commandment
and the person who carries it out, and the practice of both. Everyone must engage with these things, so that, either as someone who keeps the commandment or as someone who carries it out, he may say

these words that were written about each circumstance. It seems to me that these words become like a mirror for the person singing, so that he may reflect on them and himself see these movements of his own soul.

And so let him say them with understanding. For the person who hears the reader receives the praise as though it were being spoken about him, or as someone who repents when his conscience rebukes him and he feels remorse;
or, when he hears of the hope in Christ and the help given to those who believe,

he rejoices as though such grace were being shown to him, and begins to give thanks to God. So when someone sings Psalm 3, “Lord, how numerous are those who oppress me,” while in afflictions of his own,
[?] he regards the words in the psalm as his own. When he sings Psalm 10, “In the Lord I have put my hope; how can you say to my soul,” and Psalm 16, “Hear, holy Lord, and look upon my petition,” as
someone speaking of his own trust and prayer; and Psalm [?], “Have mercy on me, God, according to your grace,” as though he himself were speaking the words belonging to his own repentance.

But Psalm 3, “Lord, how numerous are those who oppress me,” and Psalm 55, “Have mercy on me, God, because he has trampled on my head,” and Psalm [?], “Have mercy on me, God, because my soul has put its hope in you,”

and Psalm 141, “With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with the Lord,” and Psalm 142, “Hear my prayer, Lord, and listen to my petition”—when someone sings these, he does not take the position of someone else being persecuted,
but identifies himself with the person who is suffering,

and sings these words to God as his own. In short, every psalm has been spoken by the Spirit and fitted together so that in them, as has been said, the movements of our souls may be expressed, and so that all these things, as though spoken about us
and belonging to us, may serve as our own words, to remind us of the movements within us
and to correct our conduct. For the things spoken by those who sang them can also become ours, and serve as a pattern and an image.

This too is the Savior’s grace. For when he became human for our sake, he offered his own body to death on our behalf, so that he might rescue us all from death. And when he wished to show us a way of life
that was heavenly and acceptable, he provided an example in this very thing, so that people would no longer be easily led astray by the enemy, since they have as a pledge for their protection
the victory he won for us against the enemy. For this reason, then, he not only taught,
but also did what he taught, so that everyone might hear him speaking and, looking at him as at an image, take from him an example of what to do,

when hearing, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” No one can find anything more complete for instruction in virtue than the example the Lord provided in himself. For whether it is patience, love for humanity, kindness, courage, or righteousness,
or mercy, one finds these in him, so that anyone who reflects on the Lord’s human way of life will lack nothing needed for virtue. Knowing this, Paul said,
“Be imitators of me, as I too am of Christ.” For those who make laws among the pagans go only so far as to say that they have good [?]
But the Lord, who truly is Lord of all and cares for all these things that he made, [?] not only laid down a law but also gave himself as its pattern, so that [?] might know
the power to act, those who wish to do so. For this reason, even before his coming [?] to us, he [?] this through those who sing, so that, just as in himself he taught by portraying a human being [?]
perfect and heavenly, so anyone wishing to learn can also learn from the psalms these movements [?] and dispositions of souls, finding in them [?]
both healing and correction for every movement. For, if it is right to speak more persuasively [?] disposition.

Every book of divine Scripture teaches the virtue of true faith, but the Book of Psalms also contains, in a certain way, an image of the life of souls. For just as someone entering the king’s presence
is instructed in both bearing and speech, so that he does not speak in a way contrary to these instructions
and get thrown out as an uncultivated person, so divine Scripture, for someone who pursues virtue and wishes to reflect on the Savior’s bodily way of life,

It first calls to mind, through reading, the movement of the soul, and thus goes on to give examples and teach those who encounter words of this kind. They are, then, as someone first observed this about the book [?]. Some of them
are spoken in narrative form, some in exhortation, some in prophecy, some as prayer, and some as confession. Those in narrative form are these:

Psalm 18: “The heavens recount the glory of God.” Psalm 70: “God, we have heard with our ears.” Psalm 48: “Hear this, all you peoples.” Psalm 49: “God, the God of gods, [?] has spoken.” Psalm 72: “God is good to Israel and to the pure in heart.”

Psalm 77: “My people, listen to my law and be persuaded.” Psalm 86: “His foundations are on his holy mountain.” Psalm 88: “I will sing of the Lord’s grace forever.” Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” Psalm 113: “When Israel came out

of Egypt.” Psalm 126: “Unless the Lord builds the house.” Psalm 136: “By the rivers of Babylon.” Those that are in the form of prayer: Psalm 16: “Hear, holy Lord, and look upon my petition.” Psalm 67: “Let God arise, and let

all his enemies be scattered.” Psalm 110: “Lord, you have been a dwelling place for us throughout the generations.” Psalm 101: “Lord, hear my prayer.” Psalm 107: “Lord, remember David and all his humility.” Psalm 141: “With my voice I called to the Lord.”

Those that are in the form of complaint and petition: Psalm 5: “Listen to my words, Lord, and understand my meditation.” Psalm 6: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” Psalm 7: “Lord God, in you I have put my hope;
save me.” Psalm 12: “How long will you forget me, Lord? Forever?” Psalm 11: “Save, Lord, for the good have disappeared.” Psalm 15: “Protect me, God, for I have trusted in you.” Psalm 24:

“To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Psalm 27: “To you, Lord, I have called; my God, do not be silent toward me.” Psalm 34: “In you, Lord, I have put my hope; may I never be put to shame.” Psalm 34:

“Lord, plead my case, and fight against those who fight against me.” Psalm 37: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” Psalm 102: “God, plead my case and vindicate my claim.” Psalm 53: “God, save me by your name.” Psalm 54: “Listen to my prayer, God, and do not disregard my petition.”
Psalm 55: “Have mercy on me, God, for he has trampled me on the head.” Psalm 56: “Have mercy on me, God, for my soul puts its hope in you.” Psalm 18: “Rescue me from my enemies, God.” Psalm 59:
“God, you have forgotten us, driven us away, and been angry with us.” Psalm 60: “Hear my prayer, God, and listen to my petition.” Psalm 90: “Hear my voice, God, as I plead with you.” Psalm 82:
“God, who is like you?” Psalm 85: “Incline your ear, Lord, and answer me.” Psalm 87: “Lord, God of my salvation.” Psalm 139:

“Rescue me, Lord, from the evil person.” Psalm 140: “Lord, I have called to you; answer me.” Psalm 142: “Hear my prayer, Lord, and listen to my petition.” These are in the form of complaint and thanksgiving:
Psalm [?]: “Lord, you have searched me and known me.” Those that are in the form of complaint alone: Psalm 3: “Lord, how numerous are my oppressors!” Psalm 55:
“Vindicate me, Lord, for I have walked in my integrity.” Psalm [?]: “Save me, God, because
the waters have reached my soul.” Psalm 69: “God, rescue me; Lord, stay to help me.”
Psalm 70: “In you, Lord, I have put my hope; may I never be put to shame.” Psalm 73: “God, why have you forgotten us forever?” Psalm 78: “God, the nations have entered your inheritance.” Psalm 79:
“Shepherd of Israel, listen.” Psalm 108: “God of my praise, do not be silent.” Psalm 112: “Praise him, servants of the Lord.” Psalm 129:

“From the depths I called to you, Lord, and you heard my voice.” Psalm 130: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up.” Those in the form of confession: Psalm [?]: “Have mercy on me, God, according to your grace.” Those that contain confession mingled [?] with petition: Psalm 9:

“I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart.” Psalm 74: “We give thanks to you, God.” Psalm 104: “Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name.” Psalm 105: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his grace lasts forever.” Psalm 106:

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his grace lasts forever.” Psalm 117: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his mercies last forever.” Psalm 135: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his mercies last forever.” Psalm 136: “By the rivers of Babylon.”
Those that contain confession and narrative together with praise: Psalm 110: “I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart.”
Those in the form of exhortation: Psalm 36: “Do not envy the wicked.” Those in the form of prophecy: Psalm 20:

“Lord, the king will rejoice in your strength.” Psalm 21: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Psalm 47: “My heart has poured forth good words.” Psalm 46: “Clap your hands, all you peoples.” Psalm 71:

“God, give your judgment to the king.” These convey information together with prophecy. Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” The following are exhortations and are like commands. Psalm 88: “Bring to the Lord, sons of rams.” Psalm 30: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous.” Psalm 80: “Praise God, who strengthens us.” Psalm 94:
“Come, let us praise the Lord.” Psalm 95: “Sing a new song to the Lord.” Psalm 96: “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice.” Psalm 91: “Sing a new song to the Lord.” Psalm 98:
“The Lord reigns; let the peoples tremble.” Psalm 103: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” Psalm 106: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, and his kindness lasts forever.”
Psalm 108: “God of my praise, do not remain silent.” Psalm 113: “When Israel went out from Egypt.” The following were spoken as exhortations together with praise. Psalm 149: “Sing to the Lord a song
that is new.” These belong to those that prescribe virtuous conduct. Psalm 107: “Give thanks to the Lord and call on his name.” Psalm 111:

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” Psalm 108: “God of my praise, do not remain silent.” Psalm 126: “Unless the Lord builds the house.” Psalm 132: “How good and how pleasant!” The following express praise. Psalm [?]:
“He dwells in the shelter of the Most High.” Psalm 112: “Praise him, servants of the Lord.” Psalm 116: “Praise the Lord, all you nations.”
Psalm 134: “Praise the name of the Lord.” Psalm 144: “I will exalt you, my Lord the King.” Psalm 145: “Praise the Lord, my soul.” Psalm 146:
“It is good and pleasant to sing praises to our God.” Psalm 147: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem.” Psalm 148: “Praise the Lord from heaven.” Psalm 150:
“Praise the Lord in his sanctuary.” These belong to the thanksgivings. Psalm 8: “Lord, our Lord, how glorious is your name throughout the earth!” Psalm 17:
“I love you, Lord, my strength and my confidence.” Psalm 29: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up.” Psalm 33: “I will bless the Lord at all times.” Psalm 45:
“Our God is our mighty refuge.” Psalm 82: “My God, you are my God; I will wait for you.” Psalm 76: “With my voice I called to God, and he heard me.” Psalm 84:
“Lord, you have shown favor to your land.” Psalm 117: “I have loved that the Lord should hear the voice of my petition.” Psalm 115: “I believed and spoke, and I was greatly humbled.”
[?] “I will lift my eyes to the mountain.” Psalm 121: “I rejoiced when they said to me.” Psalm 123:

“If it had not been the Lord who stood by us.” Psalm 125: “When the Lord brings back the captives of Zion.” Psalm 128: “My oppressors have been many since my youth.” Psalm 143: “Blessed is the Lord, who trained my hands for battle.” The following speak of blessedness. Psalm 1:

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked.” Psalm 31: “Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven.” Psalm 40: “Blessed is the one who considers the poor.” Psalm 118: “Blessed are those whose way is blameless.” Psalm 127:
“Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord.” Another expresses cheerfulness together with praise. Psalm 107:
“My heart is ready, God; my heart is ready.” It belongs to those that encourage courage.

Psalm 10: “In the Lord I have placed my hope; how can you say to my soul?” The following accuse the wicked and those who transgress the law. Psalm 2: “Why have the nations been in an uproar?” Psalm 13: “The wicked man has said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” Psalm 35: “The wicked man devises wickedness in his heart.” Psalm 51:

“Why do you boast of evil, mighty man?” Psalm 52: “The wicked man has said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” The following belongs to the invocations. Psalm 4: “When I called you, you answered me.” The following express mercy
Psalm 19: “May the Lord answer you on the day of distress.” Psalm 63: “Hear my voice, God, as I plead.” The following belong to those that express words of boasting in the Lord. Psalm 22:

“The Lord will shepherd me; I will lack nothing.” Psalm 26: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” Psalm 38: “To the Lord: I will guard my way and not sin with my tongue.” Psalm 39:
“I have earnestly hoped in the Lord.” Psalm 40: “Like a deer that cries out for streams of water.” Psalm 61: “My soul waits for God, for my salvation comes from him.” Psalm 75:
“God is known in Judah.” Psalm 83: “How lovely are your dwellings, mighty Lord!” Psalm 96: “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice.” Psalm 98:
“The Lord reigns; let the peoples tremble.” Psalm 111: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” The following are rebukes. Psalm 57: “Do you truly speak righteousness?” Psalm 81:
“God stands in the assembly of angels.” These belong among those that speak words of praise. Psalm 47: “Great is our Lord, and greatly praised.” Psalm 60:
“Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” These, however, are expressions of a shout, and concern the resurrection: Psalm 65, “Praise God, all the earth,” and another that speaks words of a shout
alone: Psalm 99, “Praise the Lord, all the earth.” Such, then, is the arrangement, and the psalms [?] can [?] those who encounter them to find [?].

As I said before, and the movements [?] of their souls, and likewise the pattern, and concerning each one, and what instruction [?] can please the Creator, and by which words someone can set himself right
and give thanks to God, so that the person who speaks such words may not fall into wickedness. For we must give an account at the judgment not only for our deeds but also for an idle word.

And if [?] you want to pronounce someone blessed, you have expressions showing how it is fitting to do so, concerning whom, and which people it is fitting to call blessed: [?] “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked
.” [?] Psalm 31: “Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven.” [?] Psalm 40: “Blessed is the one who considers the poor.” Psalm 111: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” Psalm 118:
“Blessed are those whose way is blameless.” Psalm 127: “Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord.”
And if you wish to condemn the Jews’ plot against Christ, you have [?] Psalm 2: “Why have the nations raged?” But if you are persecuted by your own people, and many rise against you, you have

Psalm 3: [?] “How numerous your oppressors have become!” But if, while you are afflicted in this way, you have called upon the Lord, and, having been heard, you want to give thanks, sing Psalm 4: “When I called you, you answered me,” and Psalm 140:

“Lord, I have called you; answer me,” and Psalm 10: “In the Lord I have put my hope; how can you say to my soul,” and Psalm 114: “I have loved that the Lord should hear the voice of my petition.” And if, when you see wicked people wanting to lie in ambush, you want your prayer to be heard, rise early in the morning
and sing Psalm 5: “Listen to my words, Lord; understand my meditation.” But when you become aware of the Lord’s threat, if you see that you are troubled because of it, you can say Psalm 6:
“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and Psalm 37: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”
But if people plot against you, as Ahithophel did against David, and someone tells you this, sing Psalm 7:
“Lord my God, in you I have put my hope; save me,” and trust in God, who rescues you. And when you see the Lord’s goodness displayed everywhere,

and the human race redeemed, if you want to cry out to the Lord, sing Psalm 8: “Lord, our Lord, how glorious is your name in all the earth!” But again, if you wish to sing thanksgiving concerning the winepresses, you have that same Psalm 8:
“Lord, our Lord, how glorious is your name in all the earth,” and Psalm 80: “Praise God, who strengthens us.”

And because the enemy has been brought to nothing and creation has been redeemed, without boasting [?] in yourself, but knowing that the Son of God has accomplished this for you, say Psalm 9: “I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart,” which is spoken about him.

And if someone wants to unsettle you and make you afraid, put your confidence in the Lord and sing Psalm 10: “In the Lord I have put my hope; how can you say to my soul?” But when you see the [?] of many and the wickedness of many, so that nothing

holy remains among human beings, take refuge in the Lord yourself, and sing Psalm 11: “Save, Lord, for the good person is no more.” But when [?] from the enemies continues for a long time, do not lose heart, as though the Lord had forgotten you, but appeal to the Lord,

singing Psalm 12: “How long will you forget me, Lord? Forever?” But when you hear people blaspheming against providence, do not share in their wickedness. Instead, as you protest against them, say Psalm 13: “The wicked person has said in his heart, ‘There is no God,’” and Psalm 52:
“The wicked person has said in his heart.” And now, if you want to learn what a citizen of the kingdom of heaven is like, sing Psalm 14:
“Lord, who may dwell in your tent?” And if you need prayer because of those who stand against you and have seized your life, sing Psalm 16:
“Hear, holy Lord, and look upon my petition,” and Psalm 85: “Incline your ear, Lord, and answer me,” and Psalm 87: “Lord, God of my salvation,” and Psalm 140: “Lord, I have called you; answer me.”

But do you want to learn how Moses prayed? You have Psalm 89: “Lord, you have been our dwelling place throughout all generations.” But if you have been saved from your enemies and rescued from those who pursue you, sing Psalm 17: “I love you, Lord, my strength and my confidence.”

You [?] at the order of creation, and at the grace and providence within it, and at the priestly commandment of the law. Let us sing Psalm [?]: “The heavens tell of the glory of God,” and Psalm 23: “The earth belongs to the Lord, with all that fills it,” and Psalm 58: “Bring to the Lord, you offspring of rams.”

But when you see those who are distressed, [?] these people as you pray and say to them the words in Psalm 59: “May the Lord answer you on the day of distress.” Do you see for yourself that the Lord is shepherding you and making you prosper? When you consider
this, sing Psalm 52 as well: “The Lord will shepherd me, and I will lack nothing.” Enemies are around you.
But when you lift your soul to God, sing Psalm 24: “To you, Lord, I have lifted my soul.” And you see those perverse people acting vainly.
The enemies persist and accomplish nothing. But when their hands are full of blood and they seek to cast you down and destroy you, do not entrust judgment to a human being.
For all human affairs are subject to [?]. But when you judge that it is right for judgment to belong to God—for he alone is righteous—recite Psalm 25:
“Judge me, Lord, because I have walked in integrity”; and Psalm 34: “Plead my case, Lord, and fight against those who fight against me”; and Psalm 42: “Plead my case, God, and vindicate me.”

But if they become still more fiercely arrayed against you, and the enemies are numerous like armies, and they despise you as though you had not yet been anointed, and for this reason seek to fight against you,
do not be afraid. Instead, sing Psalm 26 as well: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

But because human nature is weak, if, again, the schemes are not concealed [?], so that you have no dealings with them, cry out to God, reciting Psalm 27: “To you, Lord, I have called. You are my God; do not remain silent.”

✝ And if, when you receive grace, you want to learn how we ought to make an offering to the Lord, reflect with understanding and sing Psalm 28: “Bring to the Lord, you offspring of rams.” ✝ And then, when you renew your house—your soul,

which receives the Lord—and also the material house in which you dwell bodily, give thanks and recite Psalm 59: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up,” and Psalm 185 among the Songs of Ascents: “Unless the Lord builds the house.”
But whenever you see for yourself that you are hated and persecuted for the truth by all your friends and relatives, do not dwell on these things or become discouraged.

Nor should you be afraid if acquaintances turn their faces away. Instead, withdraw from these things, consider what is to come, and sing Psalm 70: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; may I never be put to shame.”
When you see those who are baptized and delivered from a corruptible mind, and you marvel at God’s love for humanity, sing Psalm 31 concerning them:
“Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven.” And whenever you want to sing with many people, gathering together valiant, righteous men who are upright in their conduct, recite Psalm 32:

“Praise the Lord, you righteous.” But when you have fallen among enemies and wisely escaped from them and avoided this scheme, if you want to give thanks, as I call upon humble men, sing concerning them Psalm
33: “I will bless the Lord at all times.” And if you see the shamelessness of the perverse in their wickedness,
do not suppose that wickedness is in them by nature, as the heretics say. Instead, sing Psalm
35: “The wicked person devises wrongdoing in his heart.” And you see that they themselves are the cause of their sinning.
But if you see evil and lawless, perverse people doing many things against the lowly,
and you want to admonish people not to stand gazing at them or to envy them, because they quickly fade away, sing Psalm 36 both for yourself and for others:
